title: English Vocabulary 4 · Units 71–72
description: Advanced vocabulary for quantitative trends, statistics, estimates, formal permission, official approval and prohibitions.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal language study. Vocabulary choices are checked against the teaching units, exercises and answer key; explanations, translations and example sentences were independently written without reproducing textbook passages or activities.

audit.scope: Complete teaching pages, tables, usage notes, exercises 71.1–71.4 and 72.1–72.3, and answer-key entries for Units 71–72.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA is supplied only for short entries where a transcription was considered reliable. Longer expressions are intentionally left without full IPA. Acronym spelling is handled by speechText where necessary.
audit.languagePolicy: All learner-facing content is English, with Brazilian Portuguese only in pt fields.
audit.reviewMethod: Compared the complete unit and exercise pages with the corresponding answer key; drafted original definitions, notes and examples; checked structural schema parity, source references, uniqueness, target audio text and source classification programmatically.
audit.limitations: No bundled MP3 recordings are included. Browser import, live TTS output and speech-recognition behaviour were not tested. Some regional pronunciation and register variants may not be exhaustively documented.

units.title: Unit 71 — Number: statistics and quantity
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 71. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Describe multiplicative growth and distinguish a fold increase from an increase by a given factor.
Report numerical fluctuations and deviations using appropriate collocations and prepositions.
Interpret statistics, ratios, discrepancies and statistical terminology accurately.
Give appropriately qualified estimates and distinguish rounding, forecasting and caution.

sectionsChecked: A · Changes in numbers and quantities
B · More expressions for describing statistics and numbers

items.section: A · Changes in numbers and quantities
items.example: The revised plan delivered a twofold increase in processing capacity.
items.note: Means twice as much or by a factor of two; can function as an adjective or adverb.

items.section: A · Changes in numbers and quantities
items.example: Demand rose threefold after the service became available nationwide.
items.note: Means three times as much; often modifies increase or describes change.

items.section: A · Changes in numbers and quantities
items.example: The organisation reported a fourfold rise in annual membership.
items.note: Describes a four-times level or increase to four times the original amount.

items.section: A · Changes in numbers and quantities
items.example: Output quadrupled from 200 units to 800 units per month.
items.note: Here a verb: increase to four times the original level; not simply add four units.

items.pt: por um fator de três; triplicado
items.section: A · Changes in numbers and quantities
items.example: The response time improved by a factor of three after optimisation.
items.note: Expresses a three-to-one multiplicative relationship; identify the measured quantity and direction of change.

items.section: A · Changes in numbers and quantities
items.example: The sudden drop in revenue forced the board to introduce drastic cuts.
items.note: Used for very great, often sudden change; may imply severe consequences.

items.pt: revisar para cima; aumentar uma estimativa
items.section: A · Changes in numbers and quantities
items.example: Analysts revised their forecast upwards after stronger-than-expected sales.
items.note: Increase a previously published estimate or figure; the opposite is revise downwards.

items.pt: revisar para baixo; reduzir uma estimativa
items.section: A · Changes in numbers and quantities
items.example: The research team revised the population estimate downwards after checking the records.
items.note: Change an existing estimate to a lower figure; downwards is the British baseline.

items.pt: desviar-se da norma; afastar-se do padrão habitual
items.section: A · Changes in numbers and quantities
items.example: This quarter’s electricity consumption deviated from the norm because of the heatwave.
items.note: The fixed preposition is from; norm means the typical or expected pattern.

items.section: A · Changes in numbers and quantities
items.example: The measured temperatures deviated slightly from the predicted values.
items.note: Usually followed by from when identifying the baseline or reference.

items.section: A · Changes in numbers and quantities
items.example: The exchange rate fluctuated throughout the trading session.
items.note: Describes variation up and down over time without a necessary regular pattern.

items.pt: oscilar de um lado para outro; subir e cair alternadamente
items.section: A · Changes in numbers and quantities
items.example: Wholesale prices seesawed between sharp gains and losses over the summer.
items.note: Unlike fluctuate, seesaw suggests repeated movements in opposing directions.

items.section: A · Changes in numbers and quantities
items.example: The supplier’s erratic delivery schedule made production planning difficult.
items.note: Describes changeable behaviour or figures without a reliable pattern.

items.section: A · Changes in numbers and quantities
items.example: The estimated number of passengers using the terminal exceeded 12,000.
items.note: Estimated means calculated approximately rather than established through an exact count.

items.example: The committee examined the aggregate rather than each department’s expenditure.
items.note: As a noun, the combined total resulting from adding several amounts.

items.pt: agregar os números; somar os valores
items.example: The report aggregates the figures from all seven regional offices.
items.note: As a verb, aggregate means combine several values into a total.

items.example: Economists treated the single month of higher inflation as a temporary blip.
items.note: A short-lived deviation from a trend, rather than necessarily a lasting change.

items.example: The survey identified a correlation between commuting time and reported stress.
items.note: An observed statistical association; by itself, a correlation does not establish causation.

items.example: Gross domestic product fell during the recession despite a rise in exports.
items.note: GDP is a measure of the value of goods and services produced by an economy in a period.

items.example: The government compared education spending as a percentage of GDP.
items.note: Abbreviation for gross domestic product; usually pronounced as individual letters.

items.example: Public expenditure on transport increased faster than tax revenue.
items.note: Formal noun for money spent, commonly on or for a stated purpose.

items.example: An unexplained discrepancy between the two accounts delayed the audit.
items.note: Usually a discrepancy between A and B; suggests figures expected to agree do not match.

items.example: The ratio of applicants to available places was five to one.
items.note: Common structure: the ratio of A to B; ratios compare quantities, not necessarily percentages.

items.pt: falho; com erros; comprometido por defeitos
items.example: The conclusions were unreliable because the sampling method was flawed.
items.note: A flawed calculation, method or dataset contains defects that weaken its reliability.

items.example: The analysis combined evidence from multiple independent sources.
items.note: Means several, not simply a single large number; commonly precedes a plural noun.

items.example: The figures supplied by the contractor were inconsistent with the official records.
items.note: Use with, not to, when two data sources or claims fail to agree.

items.example: The engineers investigated a small deviation from the calibration standard.
items.note: Noun corresponding to deviate; commonly followed by from.

items.example: The auditors asked for an explanation of the discrepant values.
items.note: Formal adjective for values that disagree; linked to discrepancy.

items.example: A flaw in the methodology affected the credibility of the results.
items.note: Noun or verb; a defect or weakness, especially in an argument or procedure.

items.example: The researchers discovered an inconsistency in how the data had been recorded.
items.note: An inconsistency is a mismatch within statements, methods or evidence.

items.example: It is better to err on the side of caution when the measurements are uncertain.
items.note: Formal verb meaning make a mistake; unlike erratic, it refers directly to error.

items.example: A transcription error caused the disagreement between the two reports.
items.note: A mistake in data, reasoning or action; distinct from changing values.

items.example: The students used multiplication to check the growth factor.
items.note: Noun for the arithmetic operation of multiplying.

items.example: The article examined how communities respond to behaviour labelled as deviant.
items.note: The adjective given in the word-formation exercise often concerns social norms, not quantitative deviation.

items.example: Multiply the original value by four to obtain the final estimate.
items.note: An arithmetic verb in the word-formation exercise; compare multiple and multiplication.

items.example: Could you give us a ballpark figure for the installation cost?
items.note: Informal approximate estimate, not a precise quotation.

items.example: We still need to tot up the costs before approving the purchase.
items.note: Informal phrasal verb meaning add several numbers together; often tot up the figures.

items.pt: atingir a casa das centenas de milhares
items.example: The redevelopment costs could run into six figures in pounds.
items.note: Six figures means at least 100,000 and less than 1,000,000 in the stated currency.

items.example: Exchange rates are an important variable in the company’s forecast.
items.note: A factor whose value may change and affect a result.

items.example: The projected figures assume that energy prices remain stable.
items.note: Projected refers to future estimates based on assumptions, not observed values.

items.word: err on the side of caution
items.pt: pecar pelo excesso de cautela; optar pela prudência
items.example: When estimating demand, the planners decided to err on the side of caution.
items.note: Choose the safer or more conservative course when uncertain.

items.example: For the public summary, the analyst rounded the figure down to 2,000.
items.note: Reduce a number to a lower rounded value; contrasts with round up.

items.example: For the capacity estimate, we rounded the required number of seats up to 150.
items.note: Increase a number to a higher rounded value; may deliberately build in a margin.

items.example: The team used a conservative estimate of annual savings in its business case.
items.note: An intentionally cautious assessment, often avoiding optimistic overstatement.

items.example: The presentation warned that projected profits depend on demand remaining strong.
items.note: Future profits estimated using assumptions about variables.

items.example: They overestimated the number of visitors and ordered too much food.
items.note: Estimate a quantity higher than it turns out to be.

items.example: The initial budget underestimated the amount of maintenance required.
items.note: Estimate less than the true value; may be appropriate when giving cautious profit forecasts.

units.title: Unit 72 — Permission: getting the go-ahead
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 72. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Permission and prohibition · official and formal language
learningObjectives: Select formal verbs of authorisation and qualified acceptance with the correct complements.
Distinguish official approval, reluctant assent, tacit acceptance and approval of questionable behaviour.
Use common phrasal expressions for permission and understand official prohibitions.
Recognise the meaning and grammatical role of regardless and the vocabulary of embargoes and sanctions.

sectionsChecked: A · Permitting and agreeing that something may happen

items.pt: ceder a; concordar com uma exigência
items.example: After several rounds of talks, the company acceded to the union’s request.
items.note: Formal: accept a demand or request, often after initially resisting it; the preposition is to.

items.pt: consentir tacitamente com; aceitar sem protestar
items.example: The board quietly acquiesced in the decision despite private objections.
items.note: Formal: allow or accept something, sometimes reluctantly or without open endorsement; also acquiesce to.

items.example: Several members reluctantly acquiesced to the proposed arrangement.
items.note: Acquiesce to is an attested alternative to acquiesce in; context and regional preference vary.

items.example: The shareholders assented to the revised governance proposal.
items.note: Formal agreement with a proposal, idea or arrangement; followed by to.

items.example: Only the safety officer can authorise access to the restricted area.
items.note: British spelling; American English authorize. Implies official permission, not mere personal approval.

items.example: Authorised personnel must display identification at the entrance.
items.note: Officially permitted to act or enter; passive adjective from authorise.

items.example: The university made clear that it would not condone harassment by staff or students.
items.note: Often means accept or fail to condemn behaviour widely regarded as wrong; does not simply mean permit.

items.example: The committee would not countenance a policy that excluded disabled applicants.
items.note: Formal, especially in negatives: consider allowing or approving a proposed action.

items.example: The professional association endorsed the updated safety guidelines.
items.note: Express formal or public approval, which need not itself confer legal authorisation.

items.pt: carta branca; liberdade total de ação
items.example: The researcher was given carte blanche to redesign the survey.
items.note: Formal borrowing meaning unrestricted discretion within an assigned task; often give someone carte blanche to do something.

items.pt: dar sinal verde para; autorizar a realização de
items.example: The council gave the go-ahead for construction of a new footbridge.
items.note: Informal approval to begin an activity or project; usually the go-ahead for something.

items.example: Management gave the green light to the trial of the new control software.
items.note: Informal expression of permission or approval; the green light to something.

items.pt: proibir alguém de; impedir o acesso a
items.example: The organisation barred the contractor from entering the laboratory.
items.note: Usually bar someone from a place or from doing something.

items.pt: reprimir com rigor; intensificar o combate a
items.example: The regulator promised to clamp down on misleading advertisements.
items.note: Use on for the activity or people targeted; implies firm enforcement.

items.example: The new legislation would outlaw the sale of the harmful substance.
items.note: Make something illegal; stronger and more specific than merely disapprove.

items.example: The president vetoed the proposed amendment to the constitution.
items.note: Exercise a formal power to reject or prevent a decision.

items.example: The authorities banned visitors from entering the contaminated site.
items.note: General verb for prohibition; often ban someone from doing something.

items.example: The organisers advised against travelling, but several delegates went regardless.
items.note: An adverb, not an adjective; can stand alone to mean despite that.

items.example: All requests will be reviewed regardless of the applicant’s nationality.
items.note: Followed by a noun phrase or -ing form; of is mandatory in this construction.

items.pt: embargo; proibição oficial de comércio ou circulação
items.example: The authorities imposed an embargo on imports of the contaminated product.
items.note: Official restriction, often on trade; can be imposed or lifted.

items.example: Negotiators agreed to lift the embargo after the inspections were completed.
items.note: Lift means formally remove a restriction; contrast with impose an embargo.

items.pt: concessão; licença para operar um serviço
items.example: The operator obtained a ten-year franchise to run regional train services.
items.note: Here a legal right to operate a service for a defined period, not necessarily a retail franchise.

items.pt: tolerância zero; política de não tolerar infrações
items.example: The venue introduced a zero-tolerance policy towards threatening behaviour.
items.note: A policy that does not permit even minor instances of specified misconduct.

items.example: The government announced sanctions restricting imports of certain materials.
items.note: Official restrictions or penalties imposed to influence conduct; often plural.

items.example: The countries negotiated the removal of trade sanctions after the agreement.
items.note: Restrictions applied to international trade for political or legal reasons.
